name: Marienplatz
label: Marienplatz
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Alter Peter' (5 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Alter Peter - Aussichtsturm' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/7366154: 'Mary's Column', the best-known feature inside 'Marienplatz' (232 m across).
notes: The central square of Munich with the Mariensäule column.

text.description:
Marienplatz has been Munich's main square since 1158, and the Glockenspiel draws millions of tourists a year. The New Town Hall fills the north side, with the Old Town Hall on the east side. In the middle stands Mary's Column, put up in 1638 to mark the end of the Swedish occupation. A golden Virgin Mary tops it, a statue made in 1590 that once stood in the Frauenkirche. Four small putti at the base each fight a different beast, standing for war, pestilence, hunger and heresy.

The square photographs well because so much is packed into one space: the column, the long town hall frontage and the crowds all sit together. The most useful view is from above. The viewing platform of Alter Peter, the tower of St. Peter's Church, looks down over the whole square, with the Frauenkirche domes and the New Town Hall behind it. On clear days you can see the Alps too. Munich's official guide calls it the classic viewpoint for Marienplatz.

The climb is about 300 steps up a stair, so allow some time and a little energy. The square is busiest around the Glockenspiel shows at 11 am and noon (and 5 pm from March to October), so the ground-level shots are easier at other times of day.
text.geographic_location: Marienplatz is in the centre of Munich's old town. Alter Peter, the viewpoint, is the tower of St. Peter's Church at Rindermarkt 1, just south of the square.
text.directions_text: Munich Marienplatz station (U-Bahn and S-Bahn) serves the square. From Mary's Column in the middle of the square, walk south to Rindermarkt 1, where the tower entrance is. It is about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole view over the square. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Frauenkirche domes, the golden figure on the column or the town hall tower. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the rooftops and the surrounding streets.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (viewing platform at 56 m in the tower of St. Peter's Church (Rindermarkt 1)). An elevated panorama looking down on Marienplatz, with the Frauenkirche domes and the New Town Hall behind it, and the Alps on clear days. On the viewing platform in the tower of St. Peter's Church. From there you look north over Marienplatz, with the New Town Hall across the square and the Frauenkirche domes behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put Mary's Column near a crossing point, with the New Town Hall filling the upper part of the frame. Keep the phone level so the buildings don't lean. If you would rather stay at ground level, a head-on shot of the New Town Hall facade with the column in front works well, and the Fischbrunnen is good for a close shot of the fountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the town hall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail. Hold the phone close to the glass or barrier, if there is one, to cut reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day if you want the Alps in the distance. The square is crowded around the Glockenspiel shows, so ground-level shots are easier outside those times.

text.access_note: The Alter Peter tower is a ticketed climb up stairs, so check the official site before you go for times and entry details; the square itself is an open public space.
claims_not_in_sources: Alter Peter is just south of Marienplatz, so the view from the platform looks north over the square (consistent with the stand-here data).
A railing or barrier may be on the viewing platform, so holding the phone close may help reduce reflections or keep it out of shot.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) will include more of the rooftops and surrounding streets than the default lens (1x).
Ground-level shots of the square are easier outside the Glockenspiel show times because of the crowds.

name: Munich Residenz
label: Residenz
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hofgarten' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hofgarten' (way/150797532): middle (464 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/7456359: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Residenz' (353 m across).
notes: Former royal palace of the Bavarian monarchs.

text.description: The Residenz was the royal palace of the Wittelsbach rulers of Bavaria, and it is the largest city palace in Germany. It grew over more than four centuries from a fortress begun in 1385, so it mixes Renaissance, Baroque, Rococo and Neo-Classical styles. It holds ten courtyards and 130 rooms. For a phone photo, the palace is too big to catch in one frame from close up, so the easiest approach is to choose one side and make it the subject. The palace's garden-facing wing, the Festsaalbau, can be seen across the lawns, with the towers of the Theatine Church behind it. On the other side of the complex, the Königsbau fronts Max-Joseph-Platz. Ludwig I had it built between 1825 and 1835 in the style of the Palazzo Pitti in Florence, and it is 30 metres high. That open square suits wide shots of the long street-facing front. Spring and summer are the best seasons for the garden view, when the beds around the temple are in bloom. Keep your photos to the exterior and the gardens. The rooms and courtyards inside are ticketed.
text.geographic_location: The Residenz sits in central Munich, between Max-Joseph-Platz and the Hofgarten.
text.directions_text: The Hofgarten is reached via Odeonsplatz station, so make that your starting point and walk into the park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the garden view of the Diana Temple. Switch to telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to pull the temple closer to the flowerbeds. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) on Max-Joseph-Platz to fit more of the long front.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Hofgarten (long central allee, looking at the Dianatempel). The octagonal Diana Temple framed by the symmetrical garden paths, with the flowerbeds in the foreground. On the long central allee, and look towards the Dianatempel. The photo shows the octagonal temple framed by the symmetrical paths, with the flowerbeds in the foreground. The Residenz is to the south-west of this point, so turn that way for the garden-facing wing.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the allee in the centre of the frame so the paths lead the eye to the temple. Put some flowers low in the picture for depth. For a second view, walk round to Max-Joseph-Platz and shoot the street-facing front across the open square, keeping your phone level so the walls stay upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the temple or the palace wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and take a few frames in case of passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Spring and summer, when the beds around the temple are in bloom. Early morning or late afternoon is usually quieter, with softer light.

text.access_note: The Hofgarten is free to enter and open daily, but the palace interior and courtyards are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the Hofgarten.
The palace front is wide enough that the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit more of it in from Max-Joseph-Platz.
Dragging the exposure slider down helps stop a bright sky washing out.

name: Hofbräuhaus
label: Hofbräuhaus
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Platzl' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Platzl' (way/511751310): middle (125 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/11829267544: the OpenStreetMap point 'Hofbräuhaus am Platzl'.
notes: The best-known beer hall in the world.

text.description: The Hofbräuhaus is Munich's best-known beer hall, and it photographs well because it sits right on a small square, so you can step back and take in the whole facade in one frame. The first building here dates from 1589, when Duke Maximilian I had it built as an extension of the court brewery. Ordinary members of the public were let in from 1828, and the building was remodelled in 1897 by Max Littmann. Most of it was destroyed in the Second World War, apart from the old beer hall (the Schwemme), and by 1958 it had been carefully rebuilt. It is described as Munich's biggest tourist draw after the Oktoberfest, so expect company. From Platzl, the Orlandohaus side of the square, where Orlandostraße runs in, you see the Hofbräuhaus facade across the open space with the neighbouring Orlandohaus beside it. That gives your picture a clear sense of place and a bit of context. Walk a few steps either way until the building sits neatly in the frame. If you want a second angle, the inner courtyard and beer garden, seen from inside the complex, work best in daylight. Platzl is busy with pedestrians and traffic at most times, so keep an eye on your surroundings while you compose. Inside, the hall is crowded and people may not want to be photographed, so ask first.
text.geographic_location: The Hofbräuhaus stands on the small square called Platzl in the old centre of Munich, with the Orlandohaus as its neighbour.
text.directions_text: Head to Platzl in Munich's centre. The Hofbräuhaus is on the square itself. Once you are the building is just to the south, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade across the square. If you cannot fit the whole front in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Keep the phone level so the edges do not lean in. Use 2x for details such as the entrance and signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Platzl (Orlandohaus side of the square, where the Orlandostraße runs in). The Hofbräuhaus facade across the small square, with the neighbouring Orlandohaus in the frame. From there you see the Hofbräuhaus facade across the small square, with the neighbouring Orlandohaus in the frame. The building lies just to the south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up with the vertical lines. Include a little of the Orlandohaus at the edge to give the picture context. Wait for a gap in the crowd if you want a cleaner shot. For a different view, take a second photo of the inner courtyard and beer garden from inside the complex, in daylight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright so the facade keeps its detail. Take a few frames while people move through, and pick the cleanest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the light on the square is soft.

text.access_note: The square outside is open public space, but the beer hall inside is a busy venue, so check the official site before you go for entry details and photo etiquette.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit the whole facade into the frame when standing close across a small square.
Some patrons inside the hall may not want to be photographed, so it is polite to ask.

name: Frauenkirche
label: Frauenkirche
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Frauenplatz' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Frauenplatz' (way/4016224): point nearest the subject (128 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/225698612: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Frauenkirche' (121 m across).
notes: Cathedral with two onion-domed towers, the city's landmark.

text.description:
The Frauenkirche is Munich's cathedral, the seat of the Archbishop of Munich and Freising. Locals simply call it the Frauenkirche. It is built of plain red brick, and its two rounded domes make the twin towers easy to recognise across the city. Work began in 1468 and the church was consecrated in 1494. The towers, each just over 98 metres tall, were first finished in 1488 and received their domes in 1525. Tall Gothic spires were planned but never built because money ran out. The building is about 109 metres long and 37 metres high, and it is one of the largest hall churches in the world. It was badly damaged in the Second World War, and the last stage of restoration was completed in 1994.

For a phone photo, the best place is Frauenplatz, where you look straight at the brick façade and both towers. The church is so tall that you will not fit everything in at the default lens (1x) from this close, so switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Keep the phone level, with the gridlines on, so the towers do not lean inwards. If you want the church among the rooftops, Alter Peter gives an elevated view of the Old Town, and Luitpoldhügel gives a distant skyline view. Both are further away, and Alter Peter may charge a fee, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Frauenkirche stands in Munich's Old Town, in the city centre, and its twin towers are visible across much of the city. Frauenplatz is the square right beside it.
text.directions_text: No tram or station stops are listed for this spot, so start from Munich's Old Town and head towards the twin domed towers, which are easy to see. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole façade and both towers in from the square. If you want a tighter shot of the brickwork or the tower domes, use the default lens (1x) or the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Frauenplatz. The cathedral's brick façade and both towers, shot head-on from the ground across the square. From there you see the cathedral's brick façade and both towers head-on, straight across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the church between the two towers and use the gridlines to keep the vertical lines straight. Hold the phone upright and level rather than tilting it up, or the towers will lean inwards. For a different view, Alter Peter shows the Frauenkirche towers and the New Town Hall in one rooftop panorama. Luitpoldhügel shows the towers from far away over the rooftops, with the Alps behind them on clear days.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the red brick keeps its colour. Turn on the gridlines to keep the towers straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the brickwork looks warm and the square is quieter.

text.access_note: Frauenplatz is an open public square, but the Frauenkirche is a working cathedral and the south tower is a separate visit, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and tower access.

name: Viktualienmarkt
label: Viktualienmarkt
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Alter Peter' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Alter Peter - Aussichtsturm' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/240014249: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Viktualienmarkt' (295 m across).
notes: Famous daily food market with a beer garden and maypole.

text.description:
Viktualienmarkt is Munich's daily food market and a lively square in the middle of the city. It began as a farmers' market and grew into a favourite for food lovers, with around 140 stalls and shops selling flowers, fruit, game, cheese, fish, spices and juices. The market was set up here by a decree of King Maximilian I in 1807, and, apart from Sundays and holidays, it has run daily ever since. It also has memorial fountains for well-known Munich folk singers and comedians, such as Karl Valentin and Liesl Karlstadt, which make good small subjects.

The best overall picture is from above. The viewpoint is the tower of St. From the observation deck of the tower you look down on the stalls and the maypole, with the New Town Hall and the Frauenkirche in the wider view. The climb is about 300 steps and the tower has an entrance fee, so check the official site before you go. Once you are back down, the market is only a short walk away. There you can photograph the painted maypole between the stalls, or close scenes of produce and people at the standing tables. The maypole may not be in place when you visit, so don't rely on it. If you want to photograph people at close range, ask first.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Munich's old town, around the foot of Petersbergl, the small hill where St. Peter's Church stands.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot. The market is in the centre of Munich's old town, around the foot of Petersbergl. Alter Peter is the tower of St. Peter's Church. Remember the stalls are closed on Sundays and holidays. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: On the tower, start with the default lens (1x) for the whole market. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the New Town Hall or the Frauenkirche. Down among the stalls, the ultra-wide (0.5x) fits in a whole row of stalls and the maypole.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Alter Peter (tower of St. Peter's Church, observation deck). A high view down onto the market and its maypole, with the New Town Hall and Frauenkirche in the wider frame. Go up Alter Peter, the tower of St. Peter's Church.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the market's stalls in the lower part of the frame, keeping the towers of the old town above them. If you want a second viewpoint, go down to the market and shoot the painted maypole framed by the stalls. For a different kind of picture, try close, candid scenes of produce and people at the standing tables.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the screen on the market roofs to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stalls and the buildings keep their colour. Zoom in and out rather than leaning over the edge. For people at close range, switch to portrait mode, but ask first.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit on a day when the market is trading, as the stalls are closed on Sundays and holidays. Morning or midday, when the stalls are open and busy, will give you the most to photograph.

text.access_note: The market is an open public square, but the stalls are closed on Sundays and holidays. The Alter Peter tower has an entrance fee, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Alter Peter, the tower of St. Peter's Church, is the viewpoint for the overhead shot of the market.
Morning or midday is likely to be the busiest and liveliest time at the stalls.
Exposure may need lowering from the tower when the sky is bright.

name: BMW Welt
label: BMW Welt
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lerchenauer Straße footbridge' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Lerchenauer Straße' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/15804929: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'BMW Welt' (239 m across).
notes: Futuristic BMW showroom next to the BMW headquarters.

text.description:
BMW Welt is the glass-and-steel building beside Munich's Olympic Park where BMW shows its cars and hands them over to new owners. Its twisting double cone and the wide, floating roof make it one of the easiest modern buildings in the city to photograph, because the shapes read clearly even in a small phone frame. The architects were COOP HIMMELB(L)AU of Vienna. It was built between 2003 and 2007 and opened on 17 October 2007. The roof carries a large solar installation, and the building is described as the most visited tourist attraction in Bavaria.

Destination Munich recommends the Lerchenauer Straße footbridge as the best approach, with a classic combined view of the cone and the Olympic Tower. From there the double cone sits in the foreground with the Olympic Tower rising behind it, so you get both landmarks in one picture as you walk towards the entrance. The tower is currently closed to visitors but still stands in the frame. The bridge also crosses a busy road, so after dark you can catch moving car lights below.

If you have time, walk on to the building itself for close shots of the cone, where the roof seems to rest on it like a cloud. For a distant view of the whole BMW complex, Olympiaberg is a good alternative. Keep an eye on traffic and other walkers while you frame your shots.
text.geographic_location: BMW Welt is in Munich's Am Riesenfeld district, right next to the Olympic Park and close to the BMW headquarters and factory.
text.directions_text: Head for the Olympic Park side of Lerchenauer Straße in Am Riesenfeld. No nearby public transport stops are listed for this spot, so plan your route before you go. Take care crossing the busy roads around it, and use the footbridge rather than crossing at road level. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the cone and the Olympic Tower in one frame. Try 2x if you want the tower larger behind the building. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the building and want the full cone and roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lerchenauer Straße footbridge (footbridge from the Olympic Park side). The double cone of BMW Welt with the Olympic Tower rising behind it, framed in one shot as you walk toward the building. From the Olympic Park side you look west at the double cone of BMW Welt, with the Olympic Tower rising behind it, so both fit in a single shot as you walk towards the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the cone on one of the lower thirds, leaving the tower to rise in the space behind it. Keep the phone level so the building's lines do not lean. If the bridge railing gets in the way, hold the phone just above it. For a wider view of the whole BMW complex, Olympiaberg is a good second viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the glass is not washed out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, just after sunset, works well because the lights on the road below leave trails while the sky still has some colour.

text.access_note: The footbridge is a public walkway, but the building is an event and visitor venue, so check the official site before you go for any photo rules and event closures.

name: Asam Church
label: Asam Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sendlinger Straße' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/47515468: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sankt Johann Nepomuk / Asam Church' (41 m across).
notes: Lavish late-Baroque church built by the Asam brothers.

text.description:
The Asam Church (St. Johann Nepomuk) is a small Baroque church that is easy to walk straight past. It was built between 1733 and 1746 by the brothers Egid Quirin Asam, a sculptor, and Cosmas Damian Asam, a painter, as their own private church. The plot is only about 22 by 8 metres, and the façade is built into the row of houses along Sendlinger Straße. It curves gently outwards, with columns and figures. That is what makes it photograph well: you get colour, depth and detail in one frame, with the street and the two neighbouring houses around it. The Asams also decorated the house next to it, so the whole frontage is worth including.

Inside, painting, sculpture and architecture are packed into a narrow space. The ceiling fresco of the life of Saint Nepomuk is considered a masterpiece of Cosmas Damian Asam, and the high altar is framed by four twisting columns. The choir was badly damaged in a bomb attack in 1944 and was restored between 1975 and 1983.

For your phone, the street is the easy part: you can shoot at any time from the pavement. Take a few frames of the whole frontage, then move in for the figures above the door. If you go inside, rules on photography may vary, so check on arrival.
text.geographic_location: The Asam Church stands on Sendlinger Straße in the pedestrian zone of central Munich. It is built into the row of houses, with the Asamhaus beside it.
text.directions_text: Head to Sendlinger Straße in central Munich and walk the pedestrian zone, looking for the colourful façade set into the row of houses. Access from the street is by steps. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because you are close and the street is narrow, and it fits the whole façade and the neighbouring houses. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a straighter, more natural view of the portal. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the columns and figures above the door.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the best view, stand on the pavement of Sendlinger Straße on the opposite side of the street, facing the portal. From here you see the church's colourful façade with its columns and figures, set between the neighbouring houses. This frontal view is the best one, since the church has no open square in front of it and no distant view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the portal up with the centre of the frame so the curved front looks balanced. Keep the two neighbouring houses on either side to show how the church is squeezed into the row. If people walk through, wait a moment or include them to show the scale. If you go inside, the other classic shot is the gilded altar and the painted ceiling, framed by the narrow nave. Try it from the back of the nave, which still shows most of the interior.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the colours and gilding stay rich. Inside, hold the phone steady against a pillar or your body, keep the flash off, and use night mode if the phone offers it. If photography is allowed, tripods are not needed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Avoid church services, when sightseeing inside is not possible.

text.access_note: The façade can be photographed from the public pedestrian street, but the church is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and photography rules inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Strong sun or bright sky can make the façade look washed out unless exposure is lowered slightly.

name: Deutsches Museum
label: Deutsches Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3866522: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'German Museum' (425 m across).
notes: The world's largest museum of science and technology, on an Isar island.

text.description:
The Deutsches Museum is the world's largest museum of science and technology, with about 125,000 objects from 50 fields, and it is the largest museum in Munich. It sits on a small island in the River Isar. The island was once called Kohleninsel (coal island) and was renamed Museumsinsel when the city gave it to the museum in 1903. Before 1772 nothing was built there because the river flooded it so often. The museum opened its permanent building on 2 May 1925, and by the end of 1944 bombing had damaged about 80% of its buildings.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the sheer scale of the site. The phone icon on the map is right in the middle of the museum grounds, so you are inside the subject rather than looking at it from far away. That suits close-up pictures of façades, entrances, signs and the river setting better than one picture of the whole complex. The museum outline is about 425 m across, so a single frame will not hold all of it. Take a few separate shots instead: a wide one of the nearest building, a tighter one of an architectural detail, and one looking out towards the water. Turn on gridlines so the vertical edges of the buildings stay straight. Check the official site before you go if you also want to photograph inside, as rules for photography and entry can differ.
text.geographic_location: The museum is on the Museumsinsel, a small island in the River Isar in central Munich. The island is surrounded by the river and sits close to the city centre.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is named for this spot, so use a map app to reach the Museumsinsel, the island in the River Isar in central Munich. Once you are on the island, walk to the phone icon on the map in the middle of the museum grounds. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for façades and entrances when you are close to the buildings. Use the default lens (1x) for most general shots. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as windows, signs and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Pick the building or entrance nearest to you and photograph that. If you want a fuller view of a building, walk a little way towards the edge of the grounds and turn round.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use gridlines to keep the building edges upright. Keep the camera level and avoid tilting the phone upwards, as this makes tall walls lean inwards. Use the telephoto for a few close, detailed shots. Include a bit of sky or river in some frames to show the island setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then use the exposure slider to bring down bright sky so the stonework keeps its detail. If the scene looks flat, take one wide shot and one close shot and compare them.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a bright but not harsh part of the day, such as morning or late afternoon, when the building fronts are lit evenly. Check the official site for visiting times before you go.

text.access_note: Check the official museum website for entry conditions and photography rules before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and more even on building fronts than harsh midday sun.
Photography rules and entry conditions may differ inside the museum from those outside.
Pointing the phone upwards makes tall walls appear to lean inwards.

name: English Garden
label: English Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Monopteros' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Monopteros' (node/13718228408): point; moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/159075298: large area 'English Garden' (5861 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: One of the largest city parks in the world, with the Eisbach surf wave.

text.description: The English Garden is one of the world's largest city parks, covering about 3.7 square kilometres and running from central Munich out towards the north-eastern city limits. Work began in 1789 for Elector Charles Theodore, and the park was officially opened to the public in 1792. It was laid out in the informal English landscape style, so you get open meadows, streams and big trees rather than formal beds. That is why it photographs well: wide green space with a soft, natural look. The park is far too big for one picture, so this spot is a single vantage point, the Monopteros. This temple stands on an artificial hill, which was added after Sckell's time by his nephew Carl August Sckell. The temple was damaged by bombing in the Second World War. From the temple's platform, or from the grass slope below it, you look out over the meadows and the tree canopy towards the towers of central Munich, including the Frauenkirche. The best pictures put the green foreground first and the towers as a distant line. If you have time, two other places in the park are worth a look: the Chinesischer Turm, a wooden pagoda among tall trees and beer-garden tables, and the Eisbachwelle, where surfers ride a standing wave. Take a few frames at different zoom levels and keep the skyline level.
text.geographic_location: The English Garden lies in the north-east of central Munich. It stretches from the edge of the city centre out towards the city limits, and the Monopteros stands on its hill within the park.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is given for this spot, so check a map for the best route. The English Garden lies to the north-east of central Munich. Allow extra time to walk up the grass slope. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole view of meadow, trees and distant towers. Switch to 2x or 3x telephoto, depending on your phone, to bring the Frauenkirche and the other towers closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the temple itself and the sweep of the slope.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Monopteros (on the artificial hill, from the temple's platform or the grass slope below it). Looking out from the hilltop temple, the wide English Garden meadows and tree canopy lead toward the towers of central Munich, including the Frauenkirche. From here the wide English Garden meadows and the tree canopy lead your eye towards the towers of central Munich, including the Frauenkirche.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, with the meadow filling the foreground. Use the telephoto to pick out the towers above the trees. For a variation, use 0.5x and include a column or edge of the temple as a frame. The Chinesischer Turm or the Eisbachwelle make a good second stop in the park.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Hold the phone steady against the temple column or rail, and take a few frames to be sure one is sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour before sunset. In summer, arrive 30 to 45 minutes early to get a spot on the slope.

text.access_note: The Monopteros is an open-air public place, but check the official site before you go for current conditions and any entry fee.

name: Nymphenburg Palace
label: Nymphenburg Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Badenburg' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Badenburg' (node/10026962983): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3189375851: the OpenStreetMap point 'Nymphenburg Palace'.
notes: Baroque summer palace of the Bavarian rulers with a large park.

text.description:
Nymphenburg Palace is a Baroque summer residence of the former Bavarian rulers, the Wittelsbachs, in Munich's western district of Neuhausen-Nymphenburg. It was commissioned in 1664 by Ferdinand Maria and Henriette Adelaide of Savoy, and the central pavilion was finished in 1675. Later rulers added pavilions, gallery wings and a sweeping circle of lodges in front. The whole frontage is about 632 m wide, which is wider than Versailles. The park was opened to the public in 1792, and King Ludwig II was born here in 1845.

Most people head straight for the palace front across the long canal. For something calmer, this spot is on the lakeside in the southern part of the park, with the small Badenburg pavilion as your backdrop. Benches along the water make it easy to pause and line up a shot, and it is usually far quieter than the palace forecourt. The pavilion sits against still water and trees, so the picture feels peaceful rather than grand.

Take a few frames here, then walk on towards the palace for the classic view of its full front at the end of the canal, with its reflection in the water. The palace interior is ticketed, and park hours change through the year, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the southern part of the Nymphenburg Palace park, in Munich's western district of Neuhausen-Nymphenburg. The palace itself lies to the north-east of this spot.
text.directions_text: No public-transport stops are listed for this spot, so use a map app on your phone to plan the route to the southern part of the park, by the lake with the Badenburg pavilion. From here the palace lies about 800 m to the north-east in a straight line. Park opening hours vary by season, so check the official site before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the Badenburg pavilion with its lake. Switch to telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to pick out the pavilion's details and its reflection. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole lakeside with the benches and trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (lakeside in the southern part of the park, with the Badenburg pavilion as backdrop). The small Badenburg park pavilion framed against its lake, a quieter scene away from the palace crowds. The palace itself lies to the north-east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the pavilion on one of the third lines, with the water filling the lower part of the frame. Include a bench or an overhanging branch in the foreground for depth. For the classic palace view, walk north-east afterwards and shoot the full front along the canal, keeping the horizon level.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pavilion to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. Wait for the water to settle before pressing the shutter, to keep the reflection clean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the pavilion and the water, and the lakeside tends to be calmer outside the middle of the day.

text.access_note: The park is a public space, but its opening hours change with the season and the palace interior is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: New Town Hall
label: New Town Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Marienplatz' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Marienplatz' (node/2941687118): point; moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/147095: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'New Town Hall' (174 m across).
notes: Neo-Gothic town hall with the famous Glockenspiel.

text.description:
The New Town Hall forms the northern side of Marienplatz and is the most striking building on the square. It is neo-Gothic and built of brick and limestone, with a tower, pointed gables and carved detail from top to bottom. The first section was built between 1867 and 1874 to a design by Georg Hauberrisser, and the tower was added between 1898 and 1905. The main façade is almost 100 metres long. It carries statues of Henry the Lion and nearly the whole line of the Wittelsbach rulers of Bavaria, which makes it the largest princely cycle on a German town hall. The tower is 85 metres high and topped by the Münchner Kindl figure.

It photographs well because the square gives you room to step back and take it in. Look up for the details, such as the figures on the tower bay and the clock with its Glockenspiel. The figures perform at set times, including 11am and 12pm, and the square fills with people then, so allow for that. If you want a different angle, the Town Hall tower and Alter Peter both look down over the square, but they are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The New Town Hall forms the northern side of Marienplatz in the centre of Munich, with the small park called Marienhof behind it.
text.directions_text: Head for Marienplatz in the centre of Munich. From there the Town Hall is to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full façade and tower in one frame, then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower top and statues. The default lens (1x) works well for the Marian Column with the Town Hall behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Marienplatz (in front of the Mariensäule, facing the north façade). The full neo-Gothic façade and tower of the New Town Hall across the square, with the Marian Column in the foreground. From here you see the whole neo-Gothic façade and tower across the square, with the column in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it does not lean. Keep the Marian Column to one side as a foreground. If you want a view from above instead, the Town Hall tower and Alter Peter look down on the square, but both are ticketed.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white. A Live Photo can catch the Glockenspiel figures moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is quieter and the light is softer. The square gets crowded around the Glockenspiel times.

text.access_note: Marienplatz is an open public square; going up the Town Hall tower or Alter Peter is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Town Hall's main façade faces south onto the square, so around the middle of the day the sun is behind you when you face it.
The ultra-wide lens is needed to fit the whole façade and tower in one frame from the square.
Marienplatz is in Munich's old town centre.

name: St. Peter's Church
label: Alter Peter
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sankt-Jacobs-Platz' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Sankt-Jakobs-Platz' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/228534603: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Peter' (93 m across).
notes: Oldest parish church in the city, with a tower that has a city view.

text.description:
St. Peter's is the oldest recorded parish church in Munich, and many people think the city began around it. Its tall tower, known as "Alter Peter" (Old Peter), is a Munich emblem. The tower is 91 metres high and has a Renaissance steeple top, added in the early 17th century. The church stands on a small rise called the Petersbergl. A church was there before the city was founded in 1158. The building you see today was shaped by a great fire in 1327, rebuilding and a new dedication in 1368, and a Baroque choir added in the early 1600s. It was badly damaged in the Second World War.

The church photographs well because the tall tower sits above the lower rooftops and market streets around it. The best street-level view is from Sankt-Jacobs-Platz, where the facade and tower appear together and you can see the Rindermarkt side of the building. Keep the tower upright by holding the phone level and switching on gridlines. If the tower looks cut off, step back or use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x). A second option is the Blumenstraße side of the Viktualienmarkt, where the tower rises behind the market stalls. You can also shoot from inside the market itself, with the stalls or the Maypole in the foreground. The streets around the church can be busy, so wait for a gap in the people before you take the shot.
text.geographic_location: St. Peter's stands in the inner city of Munich, on a small rise called the Petersbergl, close to the Rindermarkt and the Viktualienmarkt.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so aim for the inner city around Marienplatz, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further out. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the facade and the full height of the tower into one frame. Then try the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the steeple top and the details of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Sankt-Jacobs-Platz. The church's facade and tower seen from the square, with the Rindermarkt side of the building in view. From there the church lies to the north-east, and you see its facade and tower with the Rindermarkt side of the building in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Hold the phone level and, if you can, keep the tower as the tallest thing in the picture, with rooftops or street life below it. For a different view, try Blumenstraße or the Viktualienmarkt, where the tower rises behind the market stalls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. If people walk through the frame, take a Live Photo and choose the cleanest moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer in the streets around the church. Light from the side often shows the stonework better than flat midday light.

text.access_note: The church is a place of worship, and the tower may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Königsplatz
label: Königsplatz
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Glyptothek' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Glyptothek' (relation/532621): middle (122 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5640807: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Königsplatz' (462 m across).
notes: Neoclassical square with the Propylaea and two museums.

text.description:
Königsplatz is a large, formal square in Munich's museum quarter, the Kunstareal. It is laid out in a calm neoclassical style, with the Propyläen gate at one end and two museums facing each other across the grass: the Glyptothek (archaeological museum) and the Staatliche Antikensammlungen. The three main buildings were put up between 1816 and 1845, and Leo von Klenze designed the Glyptothek and the gate. The centre of the square was set almost a metre lower than its edges, so the buildings look taller. That gives you tidy, symmetrical pictures with lots of sky and open space.

For a phone photo, start on the Glyptothek steps. From there you look down across the square toward the Propyläen, and the museum's own columns frame the foreground. It is a raised, quieter view than the open lawn. If you have time, walk down for a second shot from the square itself, where the facades face each other. A third option is Brienner Straße, where the gate closes the end of the street.

The Propyläen cannot be walked through, and it now stands on a traffic island, so keep to the pavements and stay out of the roadway. The square is often used for concerts and public gatherings, so check ahead for events, and a tripod or commercial shoot may need permission.
text.geographic_location: Königsplatz is in Munich's Kunstareal, the gallery and museum quarter. It sits along Brienner Straße, next to the Glyptothek and the Staatliche Antikensammlungen.
text.directions_text: Königsplatz is served by a U-Bahn station of the same name. If you are coming from elsewhere in the Kunstareal, head for the square on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the steps to fit the Glyptothek's columns, the whole square and the sky into one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the Propyläen. If your phone has a 2x-3x telephoto lens, use it to pick out the gate on its own.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Glyptothek (the steps of the Glyptothek, looking across the square). A raised view over the square toward the Propyläen, with the Glyptothek's own columns in the foreground. The middle of the square lies to the south-west of you. From here you get a raised view over the square toward the Propyläen, with the Glyptothek's columns in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use the columns as a frame at the edge of the picture. Keep the Propyläen on one of the grid's vertical lines, and keep the horizon level so the buildings look straight. For a different angle, try the open square, or Brienner Straße, where the gate closes the view at the end of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate or the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the stone keeps its detail. Take a quick panorama if you want the full width of the square, and hold the phone steady as you sweep.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The Glyptothek steps are a sunny spot, so a bright day suits them. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.

text.access_note: The square and steps are open public space, but the museums and any events on the square may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Chinese Tower
label: Chinese Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Monopteros' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Monopteros' (node/13718228408): point; moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W18961351 (Chinese Tower): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Wooden pagoda with a beer garden in the English Garden.

text.description: The Chinese Tower is a wooden, pagoda-style tower that rises above the tables and tree canopy of a busy Bavarian beer garden. It is a popular beer-garden landmark in Munich, and its stacked, tiered shape stands out against the green of the park. The classic shot is taken from the beer garden itself, with the crowd in the foreground. This map points you to a quieter alternative: the hilltop terrace of the Monopteros, the temple looking back toward the tower. From there you see across the park meadows and treetops, with the tower in the view. On a clear day the steeples of the old town are visible too. Guides recommend the Monopteros, and it works especially well at golden hour and sunset. The tower's interior is closed to the public, so all your pictures will be taken from outside. The scene changes through the year. Brass bands play on weekends, and a Christmas market runs in winter, which adds people and colour. The tower is a fair distance from the terrace, so use your phone's zoom to bring it closer and keep the park around it. Take a few wide frames as well, since the trees and meadows are a big part of the picture.
text.geographic_location: In Munich, in a park setting. The Monopteros viewpoint sits on a hilltop terrace, with the Chinese Tower and its beer garden to the north.
text.directions_text: Head for the Monopteros temple on its hill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide view over the meadows and treetops. Then use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is useful for taking in the whole sweep of the park from the terrace.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Monopteros (hilltop terrace of the temple, looking back toward the tower). A view across the park meadows and treetops that takes in the Chinese Tower, with the old town's steeples visible on a clear day. Stand on the hilltop terrace of the temple and look back toward the tower, which lies to the north. From here the photo shows the park meadows and treetops with the Chinese Tower in the view, and the old town's steeples on a clear day.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the tower on one of the upper grid intersections. Leave the meadows and treetops filling the rest of the frame so the tower looks like part of the park. Try one wide shot, then a zoomed shot of the tower alone. If you want the beer-garden crowd in the foreground, the other option is the tower itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the sky keeps its colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands when you zoom in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour and sunset are recommended. Weekends add brass bands in the beer garden, and winter adds the Christmas market.

text.access_note: The Monopteros viewpoint is free, and the beer garden is free to enter, but check the official site before you go for any events or changes.

name: Olympiapark
label: Olympiapark
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Olympiaberg' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Olympiaberg' (node/158712415): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/10053878: large area 'Olympiapark' (2332 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: 1972 Olympic site with its tent roof and Olympic Tower.

text.description: Olympiapark was built for the 1972 Summer Olympics on the old Oberwiesenfeld airfield, and it still works as a public park with sports venues and event spaces. What makes it a good photo spot is the mix of landscaped grass, a lake and the huge see-through tent roof designed by Frei Otto with Günter Behnisch. The roof sweeps over much of the site, and the landscaping was by Günther Grzimek. The best overview is from the Olympiaberg, the grassy hill on the south side. From the top you can fit the tent roof, the stadium bowl, the Olympiasee and the Olympiaturm into one frame, with the Alps behind on clear days. The hill needs no ticket. It is also where people have sat to listen to stadium concerts for free. For your photos, start wide to show the whole scene, then step in closer. Use the roof's curves and cables as lines that lead the eye, and keep the lake in the foreground for reflections on calm days. The Olympiaturm is closed for renovation and the stadium interior is closed for some years, so plan on exterior views only.
text.geographic_location: Olympiapark is in the north of Munich, in the Milbertshofen-Am Hart borough, close to the BMW headquarters. The Olympiaberg and the Olympiasee lie on the south side of the park, next to the main Olympic Area.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The park is near the BMW headquarters in Milbertshofen-Am Hart, so you can use that area as a landmark and head into Olympiapark from there. The main part of the park lies just to the west of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full view, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tent roof or the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Olympiaberg (summit, looking south-west toward the Alps and across the tent roof). The tent-roof ensemble, the stadium bowl, the Olympiasee and the Olympiaturm in one frame, with the Alps behind on clear days. Look south-west across the tent roof, with the Alps behind on clear days. The main part of the park lies just to the west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line so the roof, stadium and lake fill the frame. Keep some grass in the bottom corner for depth. If you want a close-up of the roof, the Olympiastadion is the other spot to try. Looking up at the translucent canopy and its steel cables gives a graphic shot of the structure. For a quieter, more natural view, try the grassy slope beside the water at Willi-Gebhardt-Ufer, though check the exact spot on the ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the roof to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try panorama mode for the wide sweep, and hold the phone steady and level while you pan.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is the popular time, with golden light on the roof and the lake. Alpine views are said to be clearest on cold, dry days after a front has passed.

text.access_note: The park and the Olympiaberg are open public space with no ticket needed for the hill, but the Olympiaturm and the stadium interior are closed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Feldherrnhalle
label: Feldherrnhalle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Odeonsplatz' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Odeonsplatz' (node/3372671294): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25505402: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Feldherrnhalle' (43 m across).
notes: Loggia on Odeonsplatz modelled on the Loggia dei Lanzi.

text.description:
The Feldherrnhalle is a wide, open-sided stone loggia on the south side of Odeonsplatz, at the end of Ludwigstrasse. King Ludwig I of Bavaria commissioned it to honour the Bavarian Army. It was built between 1841 and 1844 and modelled on the Loggia dei Lanzi in Florence. Statues of the military leaders Tilly and Wrede are part of the monument, and a sculptural group was added in the middle in 1892. The two stone lions at the front date from 1906. The loggia is also known as the place where the 1923 Beer Hall Putsch ended in a gun battle, and the site carries a heavy history as well as an architectural one.

It photographs well because the three arches, the statues and the lions make a clear, balanced shape against the open square. For a different view, Theatinerstraße gives a head-on, symmetrical shot with the loggia closing off the end of the street. From the Theatinerkirche you look over the square towards the arches, with the Residenz towers in the same frame. Keep people and passing traffic at the edges of your frame, and take a few shots a minute apart so you get one with a clear foreground.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Munich, on the south side of Odeonsplatz at the southern end of Ludwigstrasse. It stands next to the Palais Preysing and southwest of the Hofgarten.
text.directions_text: Head for Odeonsplatz in central Munich. From there the Feldherrnhalle is about 2 minutes on foot to the south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand, which takes in the whole loggia with its three arches and the square around it. If you walk closer and the building won't fit, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a close shot of the lions or the statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Odeonsplatz (from the open square, facing the loggia). The full monumental loggia with its three arches, statues and stone lions set in the wide urban square. In the open part of the square, and face south-east towards the loggia. From here you see the whole loggia with its three arches, the statues and the stone lions set against the wide square. That is the standard way to show the monument in its setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the central arch with the middle of the frame, so the loggia sits level and balanced. Leave a little open square in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a different shot, walk to Theatinerstraße for a head-on, symmetrical view of the loggia at the end of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the loggia to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour and detail. If a few people walk across the frame, try a Live Photo and choose the cleanest moment. At dusk, use night mode and hold the phone as still as you can against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon are the usual suggestions. At blue hour, when the loggia is lit up, you can get a different, moodier shot, so it is worth trying if you are in the area.

text.access_note: Odeonsplatz is an open public square, but access to the loggia and the square can be limited by events, demonstrations, filming or building work, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Odeonsplatz is in the central part of Munich.
Early morning and late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light, which suits stone buildings.
The loggia is lit up in the evening, which allows a blue-hour shot.
Turning down the exposure slider can help keep detail in stone when the sky is bright.
The Theatinerkirche gives a raised view over the square.

name: Theatine Church
label: Theatine Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Odeonsplatz' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Odeonsplatz' (node/3372671294): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25514390: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Theatinerkirche St. Kajetan' (99 m across).
notes: Yellow Italian-Baroque church beside Odeonsplatz.

text.description:
The Theatine Church is the yellow Baroque church with twin towers and a big green dome that sits opposite the Residence at Odeonsplatz. It was built between 1663 and 1690. Elector Ferdinand Maria and his wife, Henriette Adelaide of Savoy, founded it to give thanks for the birth of their son, Max Emanuel. The design was inspired by a church in Rome, and the towers (about 65 metres) and the dome (71 metres) were added by Enrico Zuccalli. The Rococo facade you see today was finished in 1768. The warm yellow colouring has become a well-known symbol of the city. The church was badly damaged in the Second World War and rebuilt between 1946 and about 1955, and a long renovation finished in 2019.

It photographs well because the facade is symmetrical and the square in front is wide and open, so the whole front fits in one frame with plenty of sky. The Feldherrnhalle and the Residence help to frame the square. If the Feldherrnhalle has scaffolding on it, keep it out of the frame. This guide covers exterior views only. The Hofgarten nearby offers a second view, with the church behind the garden pavilion.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Munich, on the edge of the Odeonsplatz, directly opposite the Residence and close to the Feldherrnhalle and the Hofgarten.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is given for this spot, so start from the Odeonsplatz area in the city centre. The church stands just to the south, about 1 minute on foot from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole facade and square, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the towers and dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Odeonsplatz (centre of the square, facing the west side of the church). The yellow Baroque facade and twin towers of the church, with the Feldherrnhalle and Residenz framing the square. Check on site how much of the facade and towers you can see.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the central axis of the facade with the middle vertical line so the towers look even. Keep your phone level to avoid leaning walls. Leave some sky above the dome. For a different angle, try the Hofgarten, where the facade or dome appears behind the garden's temple-like pavilion and colonnades.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the yellow stucco to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the facade keeps its colour and the sky does not turn white. Use the 0.5x lens only when you need the width, as the edges of the picture can stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or the hour before sunset, when the facade glows. One guide suggests early Sunday morning for fewer people in the square.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the public square; for the church interior, check the official site before you go.

name: Isartor
label: Isartor
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Isartorplatz' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Isartorplatz' (node/13289954250): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6035286: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Isartor' (63 m across).
notes: Gothic city gate on the eastern edge of the old town.

text.description: The Isartor is the eastern gate of Munich's medieval Old Town, and it is a good first stop for a quick, easy photo. Its tall central tower and the two smaller towers either side make a strong, symmetrical shape. Dates and facts: it was built in 1337 as part of the second city wall, and the main tower is about 40 metres high. It is the most easterly of Munich's three surviving Gothic town gates, alongside Sendlinger Tor and Karlstor. The gate was restored in 1833-35, and the painted fresco on the front, added in 1835, shows Emperor Louis returning in victory after the Battle of Mühldorf in 1322. Today the gate also houses a museum dedicated to the comedian Karl Valentin, with a café. For the best overall picture, stand on the open square across the road and step back until the towers and the arch fit in the frame. The surrounding Old Town streets give the gate a sense of place. The square is a busy traffic junction, so wait for a gap and keep cars out of the shot. Then walk closer for the fresco, where the tower and arches frame the painted scene. At Christmas-market time, stalls can block the view.
text.geographic_location: The Isartor stands on Isartorplatz at the eastern edge of Munich's Old Town, close to the River Isar, which gave it its name.
text.directions_text: The Isartor S-Bahn station is named after the gate and serves Isartorplatz, so it is the easiest place to start. Look for the tall central tower with the two smaller towers either side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the square, then switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the towers are cut off. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the fresco and the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Isartorplatz (across the road from the gate, facing west). The full front of the gate with its central tower and arch, framed against the surrounding Old Town streets. From here the gate lies just to the north-west and the whole front, with the central tower and arch, fits in the frame against the Old Town streets behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Step back as far as the pavement safely allows, so the towers and arch fit. Turn on gridlines and line the central tower up with a vertical line, with the arch in the middle. Wait for gaps in traffic so cars stay out of the picture. For a different view, take one from Tal, the shopping street, where the gate closes the view with the central tower in the distance. Or walk up to the gate itself for close-ups of the fresco.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the painted front keeps its colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and keep it level so the towers do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning gives fewer people in the shot. In late afternoon the light on the façade is warmer.

text.access_note: The gate stands on a public square, but the museum, café and courtyard inside may have their own opening times, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The gate is about 1 minute on foot from the stand-here point (calculated from the distance given).

name: Siegestor
label: Siegestor
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ludwigstraße' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Ludwigstraße nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/22727580: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Siegestor' (31 m across).
notes: Triumphal arch at the end of Ludwigstraße.

text.description: The Siegestor (Victory Gate) is a three-arched memorial arch topped with a statue of Bavaria driving a quadriga pulled by lions. It stands where Ludwigstraße ends and Leopoldstraße begins, on the border between Maxvorstadt and Schwabing. It photographs well because the long boulevard leads the eye straight to it, so a centred, symmetrical shot comes almost for free. King Ludwig I commissioned it. Friedrich von Gärtner designed it, and Eduard Mezger completed it in 1852. It is about 21 metres high, 24 metres wide and 12 metres deep. It was first dedicated to the Bavarian army. After heavy war damage it was only partly restored, and the inscription on the back now reads "Dem Sieg geweiht, vom Krieg zerstört, zum Frieden mahnend" ("Dedicated to victory, destroyed by war, urging peace"). That gives it a more thoughtful story than most triumphal arches. For your phone, the best angle is from Ludwigstraße, south of the arch, looking north with the arch in the middle of the frame. If you want a closer, straight-on view of the front with the quadriga above, walk up to the gate itself. For a different look, go to Leopoldstraße on the far side and shoot back along the Schwabing street. The gate sits on a busy traffic island, so cars will often creep into the frame. Wait for a gap, or come very late at night when the streets are quieter.
text.geographic_location: The Siegestor is in central Munich, on the boundary between Maxvorstadt and Schwabing. It stands between LMU Munich and Ohmstraße, where Ludwigstraße meets Leopoldstraße.
text.directions_text: Head for the Ludwig Maximilian University area at the northern end of Ludwigstraße, in Maxvorstadt. Walk to the southern side of the arch, on Ludwigstraße. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the centred view of the whole arch. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the boulevard and sky, or if you move closer to the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ludwigstraße (south of the arch, looking north toward the gate). The arch centred in the frame at the end of the boulevard, with the monument's axis running straight up the street. The arch should sit in the middle of the frame at the end of the boulevard, with the street leading straight up to it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the middle of the arch up with the centre line so the street and the monument are symmetrical. Keep your phone level so the pillars don't lean. For a close, straight-on view of the front with the quadriga above, walk up to the gate. For a different view, try Leopoldstraße on the far side. The street layout there can differ, so check it when you arrive.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arch to focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the sky down a little so the stonework and the sculpture keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid, such as a lamp post.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening is recommended. Very late at night the streets are emptier, so there are fewer cars in the shot.

text.access_note: The arch stands in the open on a busy traffic island and can be seen from the street. Take care with traffic, and check the official site before you go if you need anything beyond viewing it from outside.

name: Karlstor
label: Karlstor
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Karlsplatz' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Karlsplatz (Stachus)' (way/107975496): middle (54 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/52103816: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Karlstor' (28 m across).
notes: Medieval city gate at the start of the pedestrian zone.

text.description:
Karlstor is a Gothic town gate at the western end of Munich's pedestrian shopping street, Neuhauser Straße, where the old town meets the busy square called Karlsplatz, or Stachus. It was first mentioned in 1302 and was known as Neuhauser Tor until 1791, when it was renamed after the Elector, Charles Theodore. It is one of three medieval gates still standing in Munich. What you see now is two side towers joined by an arch. They were reworked in the Neo-Gothic style in 1861/62 and later built into the curved buildings on either side, completed in 1902. Little of the medieval look survives, but the pointed towers and the arch make a strong, simple shape for a photo.

The best frame is from the middle of Karlsplatz, facing the gate, with the square's fountain in the foreground. That puts the old and the busy new city in a single picture. If you want a second angle, walk to Kaufingerstraße and shoot along the pedestrian street as the gate comes into view. Or go through the arch and turn round on Neuhauser Straße to frame the square through it. The arch is a busy passage at most times of day, so expect people in the picture. Early morning or late evening is quietest.
text.geographic_location: Karlstor stands on the western edge of Munich's historic old town, at the end of Neuhauser Straße and facing Karlsplatz (Stachus). It marks the line between the old town and the Ludwigvorstadt district.
text.directions_text: Walk to Karlsplatz (Stachus), a main junction on the western edge of the old town. One easy way is to walk west along the Neuhauser Straße pedestrian zone until it ends at the gate. Stand in the middle of the square facing the gate. From there the gate is to the south-east, about 3 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) from where you stand so the fountain and both towers fit in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the gate alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Karlsplatz (centre of the square, facing the gate). The gate and the square's fountain together in one frame. From here you get the gate and the square's fountain together in one frame, with the gate to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the arch in the middle, with the fountain low in the foreground. For a different view, try Kaufingerstraße, where the gate grows into view at the end of the pedestrian street as you walk from the east. Or look back through the arch from Neuhauser Straße towards the square. Keep your phone upright to catch the height of the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the stonework keeps its detail. At the default lens (1x) the 2x zoom helps you pick out the towers without walking into the traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late evening, when there are fewer people and the light is softer. In the evening, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The arch is an open pedestrian passage in a public square and street, but check the official site before you go in case of any works or events.
